sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Git won not because of GitHub but because it…
sections.para: Git won not because of GitHub but because it is a standard: a way of laying out objects that any tool, any host and any person can read, and that GitHub, GitLab and a folder on a laptop all implement. sgit is the same kind of thing, and I think that is the most important thing to understand about it.

sections.label: In short
sections.para: Git is a standard. That is why it won, not any one server. sgit is one too. Encrypted objects laid out by a convention. Everything is one hash away. The key gives every name; a file is four GETs. The name says what can be cached. -imm- is for ever; -muw- is the ref. Any storage implements the read half.

sections.label: Git is a standard
sections.para: Git is not GitHub. It is a format: blobs, trees, commits and refs, named by their hashes, laid out in a way any tool can read.

sections.label: What a vault is
sections.line: A vault is a set of files laid out…
sections.para: A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention. Four kinds of object, all ciphertext: blobs, the file contents; trees, a folder's encrypted names pointing at blob and tree ids; commits, a tree id, parents, a message and a signature; and one mutable pointer per branch, the ref.

sections.label: Everything from one hash
sections.line: What makes it a standard rather than a service…
sections.para: What makes it a standard rather than a service is that nothing in a vault has to be discovered. It is all derived from the key: The vault key gives the vault id and, one way, the read key. The read key cannot be turned back into the write key, so it can be published.

sections.label: Any storage implements the read half
sections.line: Because reading is plain GETs of fixed paths, any…
sections.para: Because reading is plain GETs of fixed paths, any storage that answers a GET implements the read half of the convention: an S3 bucket, a CDN, GitHub Pages, a folder, Python's one-line file server. sgit clone --transport static reads from any of them, and sgit publish lays a vault out for one.

sections.label: A cache you can compute
sections.line: Four GETs is cheap, but a page that serves…
sections.para: Four GETs is cheap, but a page that serves one record a thousand times a minute does not want to walk trees. So the convention has a cache layer, shipped: sgit cache add <path> declares a path, and every push keeps an encrypted cache object for it at a location derived from the read key and the path.

sections.label: Why the work stays on the client
sections.line: Scion moves history, blame and merges to the server.…
sections.para: Scion moves history, blame and merges to the server. sgit keeps them on the client, and would even if the server could read the data, for the reason git did: a merge is a workflow step that needs the context of the change, the history and the policy that says who may merge what.

sections.label: The constraint that designed it
sections.line: None of this was a plan to be minimal.
sections.para: None of this was a plan to be minimal. The server cannot read a byte, so "just do it on the server" was never available: no server-side index, no server-side render, no merge the client did not make, no derived data the client could not compute from the key.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.para: Not a formal standard. No standards body; a documented format with two implementations. Not proven at Scion's scale. The largest vault in daily use is about 35,000 objects and ten agents. No blame or bisect yet.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A voice memo of mine on 16 October 2026…
sections.para: A voice memo of mine on 16 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site from a draft by the sgit CLI team; the editorial responsibility is mine.
